doc: Mission 4, LCROSS (October 9, 2009): 'The plan is to crash?' (issue #48). The crew fly it from mission control. (1) The aim, at separation (01:50 UT): on NASA's LROC mosaic of the south pole (S-lroc-wac) the Centaur's predicted impact point is nudged into Cabeus (its place and size: S-cabeus-gazetteer) with small burns; a change of speed v moves the impact point by v times the time left (9 h 41 min), the straight-line rule of a free fall seen this far out (our simplification of the trajectory). Inside Cabeus but on its sunlit floor, or outside it: lost, tried again. Time then runs fast to just before the impact (said on screen). (2) The four minutes: the Centaur hits at 11:31:19.5 UT, the shepherding craft follows 4 min 16.6 s behind at about 2.5 km/s and hits at 11:35:36.1 UT (S-lcross-nssdc); the four minutes are shown 4 times faster (said on screen; real time for the last 15 km); the player keeps the instruments on the plume, through the craft's wobbles, and catches the glints of ice in the crosshair (Space), one reading each, when a clump of ejecta crosses the view; a reading with no glint costs a pause. Too few readings at the end: lost. Climax: the four minutes, then NASA's announcement of water (S-lcross-nasa). Our simplifications, said here: the plume's ejecta speeds (no plume height found on a NASA page), the drift and wobbles of the pointing, the flashes (clumps of ejecta) and the reading rule, showing the four minutes 4 times faster, the trim budget, the spectrum drawn for the game.

texts.aim: Move the impact point into the dark floor of Cabeus: WASD or the arrows, small burns. Enter: let the Centaur go.
texts.warp: Nine hours and forty minutes to the impact: time runs 5,000 times faster.
texts.watch: The Centaur is falling ahead of us. Real time.
texts.read: Ice glints fly out of the plume: chase them with the crosshair (mouse or WASD) and press SPACE.
texts.missed_sub: That is not how it went: the real Centaur hit inside Cabeus, near the Moon's south pole. Try again.
texts.sunlit: The Centaur hit Cabeus's sunlit floor.
texts.sunlit_sub: Ice hides in the dark. That is not how it went: the target was the shadowed floor. Try again.
texts.few_sub: The shepherding craft hit before enough data reached Earth. The real one sent four minutes of data home. Try again.
texts.end_sub: 11:35:36.1 UT: the shepherding craft hit Cabeus too.
texts.dark: Missed! Put the crosshair on the glint.
texts.faint: Too faint. Wait for the plume to rise into the sunlight.
texts.early: No glint yet! The instruments pause.
texts.arm: Killa calls each instrument: press its number (1 to 6) while it lights up.
texts.flash: The photometer watches the flash: SPACE at its peak!
texts.dive: The last 25 km, in real time: steer onto the Centaur's fresh crater (WASD or mouse).
texts.dust: Dust! No water in that one.

facts.text: The Centaur hit Cabeus at 11:31 UT; the shepherding craft flew through the plume and hit four minutes later, at 9,000 km/h.
On November 13, 2009, NASA announced that the data showed the mission had found water near the Moon's south pole.

stages.doc: The mission in five stages, each sending its part of the data home (our scoring). The instruments are the shepherding craft's own (S-lcross-nasa): a visible camera, two near-infrared cameras, two mid-infrared cameras, a visible spectrometer, two near-infrared spectrometers and a photometer (the Total Luminescence Photometer, which watched the flash). The crater the Centaur made: about 20 m across (S-lcross-nasa).
